source.title: On the Role of Batch Size in Stochastic Conditional Gradient Methods
source.authors: R. Islamov; Roman Macháček; Aurélien Lucchi; Antonio Silveti-Falls; Eduard A. Gorbunov; V. Cevher

record.file_problem: The supplied text appears to contain the full paper, including appendices; no garbling or cutoff is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies effective batch–sequence scale and optimizer stepsize in SCG and reports training/validation loss under fixed token budgets, a conceptual test of batch-size effects on generalization-related held-out performance. Its algorithm and optimization setting differ from the claim's SGD-style image and language benchmarks.
record.gate_note: Own batch-size and sequence-length ablations, validation-loss comparisons, and device-batch-size comparison are included. Prior-work claims about generalization gaps, sharp minima, and other batch-size studies are cited background only and are not rows. Empirical variance and µ-KL assumption checks do not directly measure the training–test gap.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares language-model validation loss across global batch sizes at equal token exposure, testing V5 in a new optimizer setting. At fixed sequence length, equal token budgets hold training-data exposure constant while larger batches receive fewer updates. A train–test gap is not required by V5, which names held-out performance.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors derive a token-budget-aware SCG optimization bound with beneficial, approximately batch-independent, and detrimental effective-batch regimes. NanoGPT experiments support jointly adapting batch size, sequence length, and stepsize as the budget grows. They do not establish that these effects arise from a train–test generalization gap.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies momentum-based stochastic conditional gradient (Scion), with a Frank–Wolfe stepsize, on NanoGPT language-model training over fixed token budgets. The claim versions primarily concern gradient methods and test error or generalization gaps across other settings.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch–sequence product, token budget, Frank–Wolfe stepsize, model size, training sequence length, and device batch size affect reported performance. The effect of device batch size is described as small near the optimal momentum and more visible at extreme momentum.

fits_no_version.finding: Validation loss depends on training context length even at fixed global batch size, with instability for many short-context configurations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training context length affects NanoGPT validation loss evaluated at context length 1024 under a fixed token budget.

fits_no_version.finding: Device microbatch sizes 8 and 32 perform similarly; size 2 shows small numerical effects at extreme momentum.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At fixed global batch size, gradient-accumulation granularity has little effect near the optimal momentum in this Scion configuration.

fits_no_version.finding: Gradient-variance scaling, dual-gradient-norm relationships, and training-loss hyperparameter-transfer experiments concern optimization rather than any listed generalization measure.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tested Scion optimization statistics and near-optimal hyperparameters approximately follow the proposed BST scaling rules, subject to the authors' stated transfer limitations.

record.problems: The paper notes that 1B runs have some variability from PyTorch nondeterminism despite a fixed random seed. Some figures provide qualitative comparisons without exact endpoint values in the text. The study reports validation loss and optimization measures, not train–test generalization gaps. It assumes the variance constant does not depend on model size because estimating that scaling is computationally infeasible. Some hyperparameters are adopted from prior work without additional tuning.
record.rows_left_out: No reported numerical rows from Tables 2 and 3 were omitted; other table cells were not expanded because the requirements prioritize meaningful comparisons and the text identifies the near-optimal and high-batch settings. Figure-only training-curve values in Figures 3–7 were not transcribed as numerical rows where the text gives no numeric values or the rows would duplicate the reported qualitative results.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and comparison with natural-label held-out accuracy.
Width beyond interpolation and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.

Explicit fixed-epoch experiments on a defined finite corpus, image classifiers, and controlled tests of longer training, warmup, normalization, or regularization as remedies. The study does not separate optimization shortfall from a generalization-gap mechanism.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on data size or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization-gap rankings, and comparisons against norm or margin measures.
Removing memorized examples versus removing random examples.

missing.what: The second restarted configuration increases batch 256 to 1024 while keeping sequence length 1024 and halving the stepsize; it achieves approximately 0.01 lower validation loss than the restart that doubles both batch and sequence length. R13 omits this configuration and comparison.

At fixed sequence length 1024, fixed and restarted BST batch-1024 schedules slightly outperform their batch-736 square-root-rule counterparts, with jointly different stepsizes. This provides an additional adapted-recipe comparison without exact endpoint values.

record.verdict_notes: Fixed token exposure is relevant to V5's fixed-training-budget comparison; calling it a different budget unit does not by itself invalidate the test. Sequence-length-only and device-microbatch ablations do not measure the same intervention. Table 3's stepsize-1.2, sequence-1024 cell also conflicts with Table 2's corresponding cell; the shared stepsize-3.6 value used in R3/R10 is consistent.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence are not tested.
Network width beyond the interpolation threshold and test-error behavior are not tested.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity are not tested.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD generalization comparisons are not tested.

The paper varies batch size under fixed token budgets, not fixed epoch budgets; it tests Scion on NanoGPT validation loss rather than generalization gaps, and does not test image classifiers or language models under the specified recipes.
Dropout and weight decay are not varied as explicit regularizers.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to train–test gaps are not measured.
Memorized-example removal and retraining are not tested.

reader_labels.condition: 124M NanoGPT, fixed token budget 1.3B, sequence length 1024, batch sizes 256 through 4096
reader_labels.reason: Validation loss is best near batch size 256, is close at 512, and worsens at 1024–4096 for the reported settings (R3–R7); the authors also say 256 and 512 differ little (R4). This is a fixed-token Scion result, not a fixed-epoch test of the version's full claim.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: 1B NanoGPT, token budget 10.8B, batch sizes 1024–4096 with sequence length 1024
reader_labels.reason: Batch size 1024 performs better; batch size 2048 has approximately 0.005-0.01 worse validation loss and 4096 around 0.03-0.04 worse (R16–R17). The study says large batches are not inherently detrimental when batch, sequence length, and stepsize are scaled (R13–R15).
